learn.b: A C program starts in the function main. The line #include <stdio.h> loads the standard input/output library, which gives you printf. Statements end with a semicolon and blocks use curly braces.
printf prints text. Inside the text, a format specifier marks where a value goes: %d for int, %f for a decimal, %c for one character and %s for a string. Write %% to print a percent sign.
Inside a string, \n starts a new line and \t is a tab. printf does not add a new line by itself, so you must write \n when you want one.
C must be compiled. With gcc you type gcc hello.c -o hello to build, then ./hello to run. return 0 at the end of main tells the system the program finished successfully.

qs.q: Which header gives you printf?
qs.why: printf is declared in stdio.h, the standard input/output header.

qs.q: What does return 0; at the end of main mean?
qs.why: By convention 0 means success.

o: A B C on three lines
A, then BC on the next line

qs.why: Only A and C have \n, so B and C end up on the same line.

qs.why: You need #include <stdio.h> so the compiler knows printf.

learn.b: In C you must give every variable a type. The main types are int for whole numbers, float and double for decimals, and char for one character. Single quotes make a char and double quotes make a string.
A local variable that is declared but not given a value holds garbage, whatever was in that memory before. Always give variables a starting value before you use them.
learn.code:
int n;        // garbage value
int m = 0;    // safe

learn.b: A char is stored as a number using the ASCII table, so 'A' is 65. Printing it with %c shows the letter and with %d shows the number.
sizeof tells you how many bytes a type uses; char is always 1. The keyword const makes a variable read-only. A common older way is #define NAME value.
learn.code:
const int MAX = 10;
printf("%d", (int)sizeof(char));  // 1

qs.why: The type comes first, then the name and the value.

learn.b: scanf reads what the user types. You give it a format string and the address of the variable to fill. The address is made with the & operator.
Use %d for int, %f for float, %lf for double and %c for a char. For double you must use %lf in scanf, even though printf uses %f. Read several values by listing several codes.
%s reads one word into a char array and stops at a space. An array name already means its address, so you do not put & in front of it. Make sure the array is big enough.
Forgetting & is a classic bug that crashes the program. scanf returns how many values it read successfully, so you can check for bad input. Spaces in the format string skip whitespace.

qs.q: Why does scanf need & before the variable?
o: It needs the address to store the value
qs.why: scanf writes into memory, so it must know where the variable lives.

qs.q: Which scanf format reads a double?
qs.why: For scanf a double needs %lf.

learn.b: C has + - * / and %. The % gives the remainder and only works with integers. When both numbers are int, / throws away the decimals, so 7 / 2 is 3.
x++ adds 1 and x-- subtracts 1. x += 5 means x = x + 5. With x++ the old value is used in the expression first and the increase happens afterwards.

C has no true boolean in the basic language. The number 0 means false and any other number means true. Comparisons like == != < > give 1 or 0. Join conditions with && for and, || for or and ! for not.
learn.code:
int ok = (5 > 3) && (2 < 4);   // 1
if (0) { }    // never runs

learn.b: To get a decimal from two ints, cast one of them to double before dividing: (double) a / b. Casting to int cuts off decimals. The cast happens before the division.

qs.why: Integer division drops the decimals.

learn.b: An if runs its block when the condition is true. else if tests another condition and else runs when nothing matched. Only the first matching branch runs.
A condition is true when it is not 0. That is why if (x) means if x is not zero. Use == to compare and not =, because x = 5 assigns 5 and is always true.
A switch compares one integer or char against several case labels. End each case with break, otherwise execution falls through into the next case. default runs when no case matches.
If you leave out break, C keeps running the next case's code even though it did not match. This can be useful to share code but is usually a bug.

qs.q: Which value counts as false in a C condition?
qs.why: Zero is false and everything else is true.

qs.q: What stops a switch from running into the next case?
qs.why: Without break, execution falls through.

learn.b: A while loop repeats while its condition is true. The condition is checked first, so the body might never run. Something inside must change the condition or the loop never ends.
A for loop has a start, a condition and an update in one line. It fits best when you know how many times to repeat.
A do-while runs the body first and checks afterwards, so it always runs at least once. Notice the semicolon after the closing while.
break leaves the loop at once. continue skips the rest of this round and starts the next one. You can put one loop inside another to work with tables or grids.

qs.why: do-while checks after the body.

learn.b: A function is a named block of code that you can call many times. You write the return type, the name and the parameters. return sends a value back and ends the function.
C reads your file from top to bottom, so a function must be known before it is used. Either define it above main or write a prototype, which is just the header followed by a semicolon.
C copies the arguments into the parameters. If the function changes its parameter, the caller's variable stays the same. To change the original you need pointers, which come later.
A function with return type void returns nothing. A function can call itself, which is called recursion, but it needs a base case that stops it.

qs.why: Prototypes let you call a function defined later in the file.

qs.q: What does pass by value mean?

The function receives a copy of the argument

learn.b: An array holds several values of the same type in a row of memory. The first index is 0 and the last is size - 1. You can give the values when you create it.
Loop over an array with a for loop and the index. If you give fewer values than the size, the rest become 0. To find the number of elements use sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]).
C does not check array bounds. Writing or reading outside the array is undefined behavior: it may crash or silently damage other data. You must keep track of the size yourself.
learn.code:
int a[5];
a[5] = 1;   // out of bounds, last index is 4

learn.b: When you pass an array to a function, only its address is passed, so the function can change the original. The size is lost, so you pass it as another parameter.

learn.b: C has no string type. A string is an array of char that ends with the special character '\0', called the null terminator. The text "hi" takes 3 bytes: h, i and \0.
You can change single characters in a char array. Use %s in printf to print the whole string. Printing stops at the null terminator.
Include <string.h> to use strlen for the length (without the terminator), strcpy to copy, strcat to join and strcmp to compare. strcmp returns 0 when two strings are equal.
Comparing two strings with == compares addresses, not text. Always use strcmp. Also make sure the destination array is big enough, or strcpy and strcat will write past its end.

qs.q: What character ends every C string?
qs.why: The terminator marks where the string stops.

learn.b: Every variable lives at an address in memory. The & operator gives that address. A pointer is a variable that stores an address, declared with a star.
learn.code:
int x = 5;
int *p = &x;     // p holds the address of x

learn.b: Putting a star in front of a pointer follows it to the value it points to. You can read through it or write through it. Writing through a pointer changes the original variable.
To let a function change a caller's variable, pass its address. The function receives a pointer and uses a star to change the value. This is how swap works.
An array name acts like a pointer to its first element. Adding 1 to a pointer moves it to the next element, not the next byte. A pointer set to NULL points to nothing and must not be dereferenced.

qs.q: What does the & operator give you?
qs.why: &x is where x lives in memory.

qs.why: The star follows the pointer.

learn.b: A struct groups several variables, called members, into one new type. You define it with the struct keyword, then create variables of that type.
Use a dot to reach a member of a struct variable. Use an arrow -> when you have a pointer to a struct. p->x is a shorter way to write (*p).x.
typedef gives a type a shorter name. With it you can write Player instead of struct Player every time. Structs can be put into arrays, too.
Structs are copied when passed to a function, like ints. To let a function change the original, pass a pointer to the struct and use the arrow.

qs.why: struct creates a custom type.

learn.b: malloc reserves a block of memory while the program runs and returns a pointer to it. Include <stdlib.h>. When you are done you must call free, otherwise the memory leaks.
malloc returns NULL if there is not enough memory, so check before using the pointer. calloc is like malloc but sets everything to 0. Never use memory after you free it.
fopen opens a file and returns a FILE pointer. The mode "w" writes (and erases old content), "r" reads and "a" appends. Use fprintf to write like printf, and always fclose when finished.
Open with mode "r". fgets reads one line into a char array and fscanf reads formatted values. Both signal the end of the file, so you can loop until it ends.
